latin.178: Est igitur quaestio inter nos instituta duntaxat de primo peccato Adami sumpto primo modo, hoc est, de actuali ejus inobedientia, de actione illa interna & externa, qua Dei legem transgressus est actu, praecisa ab habituali corruptione, qua actionem illam secuta est: num ea nobis nascentibus imputetur? Cui quaestioni nondum negatione simplici, sed distinctione rursus satisfaciendum videtur. Est enim ejus distinguendum attributum. Potest enim animo concipi duplex imputatio. Immediata & Mediata, vel (ut idem aliis verbis dicam) Antecedens & Consequens. Immediatam voco eam, quam solam thesibus, quas tu refutandas tibi sumpsisti, negare volui; qua putatur actio illa Adami, hoc est, vetiti fructus Manducatio ejus posteris omnibus (Christo excepto) proxime, immediate, hoc ipso quod filii sunt Adami, imputari ad duas istas poenas proprie dictas, privationem justitiae originalis quam mortem spiritualem appellas, & mortem aeternam. Hanc solam imputationem actionis illius ego negavi, quia non docetur in sacris literis adaequata fidei nostrae norma, quia pugnat cum sacris literis, quia Deum facit authorem peccati, quia Dei justitiam dehonestat, quia sequitur ex ea Christum esse natura sua peccatorem, quia alia nonnulla trahit secum absurda, mirabilem religionis Christianae puritatem & splendorem obscurantia, quae utinam fratres & conservi nostri a me per theses moniti, aut non prorsus contempsissent, aut non contemptim expendissent!
latin.179: Mediatam seu consequentem appello eam, quae haereditariae corruptionis in nos ab Adamo derivatae intuitum consequitur, eaque mediante fit. Hujus enim corruptionis participatione communicamus peccato Adami, eique, ut ita loquar, habitualiter consentimus; ac propterea digni sumus, qui Adamo peccatori annumeremur. Id me Chamierus docuit Panstr. tom. 3. lib. 6. cap. 4. de poenis peccati § XVI. & XVII. Locum, si placet, quaere & lege. Huc transcripsissem (nam est insignis) nisi consulerem brevitatis. Sed tenere me non possum quin Aegidii Hunnii Augustanae confessionis Theologi celebris verba subiiciam, quibus hanc imputationem mediatam docet & explicat. Ostendit ergo (Apostolus Paulus) Lapsum Adami non immediate & per se, sed mediate & propter aliud nobis ejus posteris imputari, quia videlicet per lapsum illum polluta est natura primorum parentum, ut nonnisi peccato corruptos & vitiatos liberos procreare possint sicut scriptum est, genuit Adam filium ad imaginem suam Gen. 5. Alias si fieri potuisset, ut in posteros non vitium proprium derivaretur a primis parentibus, tum lapsus ille tanquam peccatum alienum eis plane non imputaretur. Palam igitur ostendit Paulus unum illud delictum nobis ad condemnationem cedere tantum Mediate, quatenus per delictum illud actuale introducta est in naturam horribilis corruptio, quam per carnalem generationem propagavit in ipsos posteros. Ita ut a lapsu corruptio Naturae, a corruptione naturae in nos derivata mors & damnatio perveniat, quatenus omnes peccavimus, inquit, id est quatenus ipsi in possessionem illius hereditariam devenimus.
latin.180: Ut igitur rem verbo absolvam, quaeritur, utrum primum peccatum actuale Adami precise sumptum nobis ejus posteris imputetur a Deo Justo Judice proxime, immediate ac ordine naturae prius quam inhaerenter corrupti simus? Tu venerande frater affirmas: Ego Nego. Uter rectius, sequens disputatio, uti spero in Domino, planum faciet.
latin.181:
GAR. Distinguitur imputatio peccati in Priorem, sive Antecedentem, aut Immediatam; & Posteriorem, sive Consequentem, aut Mediatam. Haud incommode sane; nec dubito, si modo recta explicatio adhiberetur, consensum hic facile stabiliri posse: si nempe utraque imputatio eodem referretur, id est, si intelligeretur de peccato Adami eadem significatione accepto, sive de actione, qua primum Adamus reum se fecit laesae Divinae Majestatis.

PL. Cur ergo consensus non stabilitur? Cur oppugnor? utramque enim illam imputationem eodem retuli, ac nonnisi de illa actione qua primum Adamus peccavit, intellexi. Id sole meridiano clarius est, & miror vocari potuisse in dubium. Illa enim ipsa distinctio, ut alia omittam, hoc clarum facit: non potest enim de peccati habitualis seu corruptionis imputatione accipi. Quis enim dicat corruptionem ante corruptionem, aut post corruptionem; mediante corruptione, aut ea non mediante imputari?
latin.182: GAR. Ita enim paria ferme faceret cum ea, quam praemisimus, imputationis distinctione in communem & singularem: ut priorem & immediatam intelligeremus, communem illam quam diximus; posteriorem & mediatam quam propriam sive singularem nominavimus. Nam certe communis illa sive immediata, quemadmodum posterior fuit prima actuali Adae transgressione, ita prior fuit personali cujusque hominis ex Adamo prognati existentia, atque adeo etiam corruptione illa, quae in singulos naturali generatione descendit; quatenus ab initio res fuerunt omnes communiter in Adamo, quo sensu dictum est a Bernardo, Adamum & Evam fuisse prius nostros peremptores quam parentes. At imputatio singularis, propria, personalis & mediata, recte dici possit corruptione nobis inhaerente posterior, quatenus nemini personaliter imputari potest peccatum istud, nisi filius sit Adami, adeoque nisi personaliter existat: neque potest aliquis personaliter existere, & pro filio Adami haberi, nisi postquam anima & corpus in unam personam coaluerunt: quae partium hominis essentialium coalitio atque conjunctio, sine dubio conceptione posterior est &c. Ergo in conceptione prima nondum adest anima, nondum homo est, nondum filius Adami: & tamen ab ipso conceptionis momento inest vitiositas in semine, quippe quod habet fomitem illum peccati, quem definiunt, inordinatam carnis qualitatem ex peccato primorum parentium traductam in posteros, &c.
latin.183: PLAC. Si paria facit, cur non contentus illa distinctione jam recepta & commoda excogitavit novam & incommodam? Melior enim est imputationis distinctio in immediatam & mediatam, quam in communem & singularem. Primo quia illa jam fuerat usurpata ab Aegidio Hunnio & Walaeo, haec vero a quo fuerat usurpata? Deinde, quia illa est in membra non re modo, sed nomine etiam opposita; quae bonae distinctionis nota in hac desideratur. Nam imputatio illa singularis dici potest communis, & vice versa communis singularis. Quid enim? nonne humana natura, corruptio haereditaria, existentia, &c. sunt omnium hominum communes? Atqui imputatio singularis, propria, personalis non minus communis est quam natura humana, quam corruptio, quam existentia (Christum semper excipio) quomodo ergo imputationi communi opponitur? Nam membrorum oppositorum alterum alterius negationem importat. Rursus imputatio communis potest etiam ipsa dici singularis, propria, personalis, siquidem communis dicitur distributive: de singulis enim personis posterorum Adae singulatim praedicatur. Quod si dicitur communis collective, utraque dici debuit communis, altera collective, altera distributive. Deinde quod commune est collective posteris Adami, id quidem de tota collectione posterorum ejus praedicari potest, sed de iis singulis, nullo modo; sicut Apostolis commune fuit collective esse duodecim; ac propterea eorum nullus fuit duodecim. Praeterea, cum per imputationem vir doctus intelligat, vel actum Judicis declarantis aliquem reum, poenaque dignum, vel ipsam poenae inflictionem, palam est inflictionem poenae esse singularem: seu enim illa sit corruptio, seu mors corporis vel aeterna, infligitur singulis. Si igitur imputatio communis est poenae inflictio, utique singularis est. Inflictioni autem poenae respondet condemnatio, seu declaratio Judicis aliquem esse reum & poena dignum. Quaero etiam, quo sensu imputatio dicatur communis & opponatur singulari? An quo sensu solet commune seu universale opponi singulari? Non differt ergo imputatio communis a singulari, nisi ut species ab individuo suo. Non est autem species nisi in aliquo individuo suo. Extra aut ante individua sua frustra quaeritur. Attamen vult Vir doctus imputationem communem diu antequam esset singularis, adeoque extra singularem fuisse. Mitto alia discrimina. Quod si alio sensu, quam fert usus, communem singulari Vir doctus opposuit, singularitatem ipse & obscuritatem affectavit, sibique potius quam Lectori scripsit. Adde quod communis videtur magis communis esse debere quam singularis: alioqui cur id nomen huic opponitur? Attamen non est magis communis, nisi velis etiam iis communem esse hominibus, qui nunquam fuerunt, nec futuri sunt. Plura non addam; nisi hoc unum, quod praetermitti non debet. Ex ratione Viri docti, qua probat imputationem singularem, propriam, personalem corruptione nobis inhaerente posteriorem esse, sequi, imputari posteris peccatum Adae imputatione illa communi, antequam sint filii Adae, & pro filiis Adae habeantur. Quod quomodo verum & justum esse possit, tibi prudens Lector, considerandum relinquo.
latin.184:
GAR. Eam existimo fuisse mentem illis Theologis, qui peccatum Adae docent nobis imputari mediate, sive mediante corruptione & vitiositate nostra. Aegid. Hunnius artic. de pecc. Quaest. 7. Walaeus Defens. Molin. cap. 8. Enimvero longe alius Doctis Viris sensus, qui hac prioris & posterioris imputationis distinctione utuntur. Quandoquidem 1. eam, quam diximus communem, priorem & immediatam, absolute negant &c. 2. Quia posteriorem & mediatam sive singularem longe aliter exponunt, ita scilicet ut eam pretendant nulla ratione ad ipsum actuale & personale Adami peccatum respicere, sed ad nostrum ipsorum duntaxat originale vitium nativamque & hereditariam corruptionem referri debere.

PLAC. Utrumque hoc discrimen aperte falsum est. Et primum quidem: Negarunt enim imputationem immediatam Aegidius Hunnius & Walaeus tam diserte, ut disertius non potuerint. Ille ait lapsum Adami non immediate & per se, sed mediate & propter aliud nobis ejus posteris imputari. Item, unum illud delictum nobis ad condemnationem cedere tantum mediate. Quid sibi vult illa negatio, non immediate & per se? Quid exclusiva, Tantum mediate? Quid est negare imputationem immediatam, si hoc non est? Hic vero imputationis illius possibilitatem negat, suamque negationem firmat ducto a Dei justitia argumento. Locum habes supra pag. 22. uti superiorem pag. 20. Secundum etiam tam aperte falsum est, ut satis mirari non possim, quomodo a se Vir Doctus impetrare potuerit, ut id proferret. Contra enim contendo imputationem mediatam ad ipsum actuale & personale Adami peccatum respicere; nec de alio peccato a me unquam usurpatam fuisse, aut, quod amplius est, usurpari potuisse.

pass_a.178: Est igitur: There is therefore a question instituted among us only concerning the first sin of Adam taken in the first mode, that is, concerning his actual disobedience, concerning that internal and external action by which he transgressed God's law by act, cut off from the habitual corruption which followed that action: whether it is imputed to us being born? To which question it seems satisfaction must be given not yet by a simple negation, but again by a distinction. For its attribute must be distinguished. For a twofold imputation can be conceived in the mind. Immediate and Mediate, or (as I may say the same in other words) Antecedent and Consequent. I call Immediate that which alone I wished to deny by the theses which you took upon yourself to refute; by which that action of Adam, that is, his Eating of the forbidden fruit, is thought to be imputed to all his posterity (Christ excepted) proximately, immediately, by this itself that they are sons of Adam, unto those two punishments properly so called, the privation of original righteousness which you call spiritual death, and eternal death. This alone imputation of that action I have denied, because it is not taught in the sacred letters by the adequate norm of our faith, because it fights with the sacred letters, because it makes God author of sin, because it dishonors God's justice, because from it it follows that Christ is a sinner by his nature, because it draws with itself some other absurdities obscuring the wonderful purity and splendor of the Christian religion, which would that our brothers and fellow-servants, warned by me through the theses, had either not wholly despised, or not contemptuously weighed!
pass_a.179: Mediatam: I call Mediate or consequent that which follows upon the regard of the hereditary corruption derived into us from Adam, and is made by that mediating. For by participation of this corruption we communicate with Adam's sin, and to it, so to speak, we consent habitually; and therefore we are worthy to be numbered with Adam the sinner. This Chamier taught me in Panstratia tom. 3 lib. 6 cap. 4 on the punishments of sin sections XVI and XVII. Seek the place, if you please, and read. I would have transcribed it here (for it is notable) if I were not consulting brevity. But I cannot restrain myself from subjoining the words of Aegidius Hunnius, celebrated theologian of the Augsburg Confession, by which he teaches and explains this mediate imputation. Therefore (the Apostle Paul) shows that Adam's Fall is imputed to us his posterity not immediately and of itself, but mediately and on account of another thing, because namely by that fall the nature of the first parents was polluted, so that they can beget only children corrupted and vitiated by sin, as it is written, Adam begat a son after his image Genesis 5. Otherwise if it could have been that proper vice was not derived into posterity from the first parents, then that fall as another's sin would plainly not be imputed to them. Clearly therefore Paul shows that that one offense yields to us unto condemnation only Mediately, insofar as through that actual offense a horrible corruption was introduced into nature, which he propagated through carnal generation into the posterity themselves. So that from the fall comes corruption of Nature, from the corruption of nature derived into us come death and damnation, insofar as all have sinned, he says, that is insofar as we ourselves have come into hereditary possession of that.
pass_a.180: Ut igitur: That I may therefore finish the matter in a word, it is asked whether the first actual sin of Adam precisely taken is imputed to us his posterity by God the Just Judge proximately, immediately and in the order of nature before we are inherently corrupted? You, venerable brother, affirm: I Deny. Which of the two more rightly, the following disputation, as I hope in the Lord, will make plain.
pass_a.181: GAR. The imputation of sin is distinguished into Prior, or Antecedent, or Immediate; and Posterior, or Consequent, or Mediate. Not inconveniently indeed; nor do I doubt that if only a right explanation were applied, consent here could easily be established: if namely both imputations were referred to the same, that is, if it were understood of Adam's sin taken in the same signification, or of the action by which Adam first made himself guilty of injured Divine Majesty. PL. Why then is consent not established? Why am I opposed? For I referred both those imputations to the same, and understood them only of that action by which Adam first sinned. That is clearer than the midday sun, and I wonder it could be called into doubt. For that very distinction, to omit other things, makes this clear: for it cannot be taken of the imputation of habitual sin or corruption. For who would say that corruption is imputed before corruption, or after corruption; with corruption mediating, or without it mediating?
pass_a.182: GAR. For thus it would nearly make equals with that distinction of imputation into common and singular which we premised: so that we would understand the prior and immediate as that common which we said; the posterior and mediate as that which we named proper or singular. For certainly that common or immediate, just as it was posterior to Adam's first actual transgression, so was prior to the personal existence of each man sprung from Adam, and so also to that corruption which descends into individuals by natural generation; insofar as from the beginning all things were commonly in Adam, in which sense it was said by Bernard that Adam and Eve were our destroyers before they were parents. But singular, proper, personal and mediate imputation may rightly be called posterior to the corruption inherent in us, insofar as that sin can be imputed to no one personally unless he is a son of Adam, and so unless he exists personally: nor can anyone exist personally and be held for a son of Adam unless after soul and body have coalesced into one person: which coalescence and conjunction of the essential parts of man is without doubt posterior to conception and so on. Therefore in first conception the soul is not yet present, he is not yet a man, not yet a son of Adam: and yet from the very moment of conception viciousness is in the seed, inasmuch as it has that tinder of sin which they define as a disordered quality of the flesh drawn from the sin of the first parents into posterity, and so on.
pass_a.183: PLAC. If it makes equals, why not content with that distinction already received and convenient did he invent a new and inconvenient one? For the distinction of imputation into immediate and mediate is better than into common and singular. First because that had already been used by Aegidius Hunnius and Walaeus, but this by whom had it been used? Next, because that is opposed in members not only in the thing but also in the name; which mark of a good distinction is wanting in this. For that singular imputation can be called common, and vice versa the common singular. For what? are not human nature, hereditary corruption, existence, and so on common to all men? And yet singular, proper, personal imputation is no less common than human nature, than corruption, than existence (Christ always excepted)—how then is it opposed to common imputation? For of opposed members one imports the negation of the other. Again common imputation can itself also be called singular, proper, personal, if indeed it is called common distributively: for it is predicated of each of the posterity of Adam one by one. But if it is called common collectively, both ought to have been called common, the one collectively, the other distributively. Next what is common collectively to Adam's posterity can indeed be predicated of the whole collection of his posterity, but of them individually in no way; just as it was common to the Apostles collectively to be twelve; and therefore none of them was twelve. Moreover, since by imputation the learned man understands either the act of a Judge declaring someone guilty and worthy of punishment, or the infliction of punishment itself, it is plain that the infliction of punishment is singular: for whether it be corruption, or death of body or eternal, it is inflicted on individuals. If therefore common imputation is infliction of punishment, it is certainly singular. And to the infliction of punishment corresponds condemnation, or the Judge's declaration that someone is guilty and worthy of punishment. I ask also, in what sense is imputation called common and opposed to singular? Is it in the sense in which common or universal is wont to be opposed to singular? Therefore common imputation does not differ from singular except as species from its individual. But a species is not except in some individual of itself. Outside or before its individuals it is sought in vain. Yet the learned man wants common imputation to have been long before it was singular, and so outside the singular. I pass over other differences. But if in another sense than usage bears the learned man opposed common to singular, he himself affected singularity and obscurity, and wrote for himself rather than for the Reader. Add that the common seems to ought to be more common than the singular: otherwise why is that name opposed to this? Yet it is not more common, unless you wish it common even to those men who never were nor will be. I will add no more; except this one thing which ought not to be passed over. From the learned man's reason by which he proves that singular, proper, personal imputation is posterior to the corruption inherent in us, it follows that Adam's sin is imputed to the posterity by that common imputation before they are sons of Adam and are held for sons of Adam. How that can be true and just, I leave to you, prudent Reader, to consider.
pass_a.184: GAR. I judge that was the mind of those Theologians who teach that Adam's sin is imputed to us mediately, or by the mediation of our corruption and viciousness. Aegidius Hunnius article on sin Question 7; Walaeus Defense of Molinaeus chapter 8. But truly far other is the sense of the Learned Men who use this distinction of prior and posterior imputation. Inasmuch as 1. they absolutely deny that which we called common, prior and immediate, and so on. 2. Because they explain the posterior and mediate or singular far otherwise, namely so that they claim it in no way looks to Adam's actual and personal sin itself, but ought to be referred only to our own original vice and native and hereditary corruption. PLAC. Both this difference is openly false. And first indeed: For Aegidius Hunnius and Walaeus denied immediate imputation so expressly that they could not have done so more expressly. He says Adam's fall is imputed to us his posterity not immediately and of itself, but mediately and on account of another. Likewise, that one offense yields to us unto condemnation only mediately. What does that negation mean, not immediately and of itself? What the exclusive, Only mediately? What is it to deny immediate imputation, if this is not? But this man denies the possibility of that imputation, and strengthens his negation by an argument drawn from God's justice. You have the place above at page 22, as the earlier at page 20. The second also is so openly false that I cannot wonder enough how the Learned man could obtain from himself to put it forth. For on the contrary I contend that mediate imputation looks to Adam's actual and personal sin itself; nor was it ever used by me of another sin, or, what is more, could it be used.

178: So the question between us concerns only Adam's first sin in the first sense—his actual disobedience, that inward and outward act by which he broke God's law, cut off from the habitual corruption that followed it: is that act imputed to us at birth? A bare no will not settle it; the attribute of the question must again be distinguished. One may conceive a twofold imputation: Immediate and Mediate, or—same point in other words—Antecedent and Consequent. By Immediate I mean the only imputation I meant to deny in the theses you undertook to refute: the view that Adam's act itself—his eating the forbidden fruit—is charged to all his posterity (Christ excepted) immediately, simply because they are Adam's children, unto the two punishments properly so called: loss of original righteousness (which you call spiritual death) and eternal death. That alone I have denied—because Scripture, the adequate rule of our faith, does not teach it; because it clashes with Scripture; because it makes God the author of sin; because it dishonors God's justice; because it would make Christ a sinner by nature; and because it drags other absurdities that cloud the purity and glory of the Christian religion. Would that our brothers and fellow servants, warned by those theses, had neither wholly scorned them nor weighed them with contempt!
179: By Mediate or consequential I mean the imputation that follows upon hereditary corruption derived into us from Adam and is wrought through that corruption as means. By sharing that corruption we share Adam's sin and, so to speak, consent to it habitually—and so deserve to be numbered with Adam the sinner. Chamier taught me this in Panstratia, tome 3, book 6, chapter 4, on the punishments of sin, sections XVI–XVII. Look up the place and read it; I would have copied it here—it is striking—had I not been watching length. I cannot, though, refrain from adding the words of Aegidius Hunnius, the noted Augsburg Confession theologian, by which he teaches and explains this mediate imputation. "Paul therefore shows that Adam's fall is imputed to us his posterity not immediately and of itself, but mediately and on account of something else—namely because by that fall the first parents' nature was so polluted that they can beget only children corrupted and spoiled by sin, as it is written, Adam begat a son in his own likeness (Genesis 5). Had it been possible that their own vice was not passed to posterity, that fall as another's sin would plainly not have been imputed to them. So Paul clearly shows that that one offense yields to our condemnation only mediately, insofar as through that actual offense a horrible corruption entered nature, which he spread by carnal generation into his posterity. Thus from the fall comes corruption of nature; from that corruption derived into us come death and damnation—inasmuch as all have sinned, he says, that is, inasmuch as we ourselves have come into hereditary possession of it."
180: To put it in a word: the question is whether Adam's first actual sin, taken precisely, is imputed to us his posterity by God the Just Judge immediately and in the order of nature before we are inherently corrupt. You, venerable brother, say yes. I say no. Which of us is right, the disputation that follows will, I hope in the Lord, make plain.
181: Garissoles (§XVI): Sin's imputation is divided into prior—or antecedent, or immediate—and posterior—or consequent, or mediate. Not a bad division; and I do not doubt that if only it were explained rightly, agreement here could easily be reached—namely if both imputations were referred to the same thing, that is, to Adam's sin in the same sense, or to the act by which Adam first made himself guilty of offending the Divine Majesty. Placeus: Why then is agreement not reached? Why am I attacked? I did refer both imputations to the same thing, and understood them only of the act by which Adam first sinned. That is clearer than noon, and I wonder it could be doubted. The distinction itself, to say nothing else, makes this plain: it cannot be taken of imputing habitual sin or corruption. Who would say corruption is imputed before corruption, or after it—through corruption as means, or without it?
182: Garissoles (§XVII): For that would nearly match the distinction we already set out into common and singular imputation: taking the prior and immediate as that common imputation we named, and the posterior and mediate as what we called proper or singular. That common or immediate imputation, though later than Adam's first actual transgression, was earlier than each person sprung from Adam's personal existence—and earlier also than the corruption that descends on each by natural generation—insofar as from the beginning all were commonly in Adam. In that sense Bernard said Adam and Eve were our destroyers before they were our parents. But singular, proper, personal, mediate imputation may rightly be called later than the corruption inherent in us, since that sin can be charged to no one personally unless he is Adam's son and so exists as a person; and no one exists as a person and counts as Adam's son until soul and body have coalesced into one person—which union of the essential parts of man is without doubt later than conception, and so on. Therefore at first conception the soul is not yet present; there is not yet a man, not yet a son of Adam; and yet from the very moment of conception viciousness is in the seed, which has that tinder of sin they define as a disordered quality of the flesh drawn from the first parents' sin into their posterity, and so on.
183: Placeus: If the two distinctions match, why invent a new and awkward one instead of resting in the received, convenient one? The split into immediate and mediate is better than into common and singular. First, Hunnius and Walaeus had already used the former; who had used the latter? Second, the former divides into members opposed not only in the thing but in the name—the mark of a good distinction, missing here. For that singular imputation can be called common, and the common singular. Are not human nature, hereditary corruption, existence, and the rest common to all men? Yet singular, proper, personal imputation is no less common than human nature, corruption, or existence (Christ always excepted)—so how is it the opposite of common imputation? Opposed members each negate the other. Again, common imputation can itself be called singular, proper, and personal if common is taken distributively: it is said of each of Adam's posterity one by one. If common is taken collectively, both should have been called common—one collectively, one distributively. What is common to Adam's posterity collectively can be said of the whole collection, but of each member not at all—just as it was common to the Apostles collectively to be twelve, and therefore none of them was twelve. Further, since by imputation the learned man means either a Judge's act declaring someone guilty and worthy of punishment, or the infliction of punishment itself, the infliction is plainly singular: whether corruption, bodily death, or eternal death, it falls on individuals. If common imputation is infliction of punishment, it is singular. To that infliction answers condemnation—the Judge's declaration that someone is guilty and worthy of punishment. In what sense, then, is imputation called common and opposed to singular? In the sense in which common or universal is opposed to singular? Then common imputation differs from singular only as species from its individual. But a species exists only in some individual; outside or before its individuals it is sought in vain. Yet the learned man wants common imputation to have existed long before—and outside—the singular. I pass other differences. If he opposed common to singular in some sense usage does not bear, he affected singularity and obscurity, and wrote for himself rather than the reader. Add that the common ought to be more common than the singular—why else oppose that name to this?—yet it is not more common unless you make it common even to men who never were and never will be. One more point must not be skipped. From his proof that singular, proper, personal imputation is later than the corruption inherent in us, it follows that Adam's sin is imputed to the posterity by that common imputation before they are sons of Adam or counted as such. How that can be true and just I leave you, prudent reader, to weigh.
184: Garissoles: I take that to have been the mind of those theologians who teach that Adam's sin is imputed to us mediately—through our corruption and viciousness as means (Aegidius Hunnius, article on sin, Question 7; Walaeus, Defense of Molinaeus, chapter 8). But the learned men who use this prior/posterior imputation distinction mean something quite different. (1) They absolutely deny what we called the common, prior, immediate imputation, and so on. (2) They explain the posterior, mediate, or singular far otherwise—claiming it in no way looks to Adam's actual personal sin, but must be referred only to our own original vice and native hereditary corruption. Placeus: Both differences are plainly false. First: Hunnius and Walaeus denied immediate imputation as expressly as speech allows. Hunnius says Adam's fall is imputed to us his posterity not immediately and of itself, but mediately and on account of something else—and that that one offense yields to condemnation only mediately. What does not immediately and of itself mean? What does the exclusive only mediately mean? If that is not denying immediate imputation, what is? As for this writer, he denies even the possibility of that imputation and props the denial with an argument from God's justice; see above, page 22 (and earlier, page 20). The second difference is so openly false I cannot wonder enough how the learned man brought himself to say it. On the contrary I maintain that mediate imputation looks to Adam's actual personal sin itself; I have never used it of another sin, nor—what is more—could it be so used.
